name: Chácobo
confidence_why: Tallman's 2018 reference grammar describes Chácobo as a mixed tone-stress language with a lexical high tone and predictable stress on the first syllable of the stem (or the second when it carries the high tone), Tallman and Elías-Ulloa 2020 measured stress and tone as coexisting, and the older descriptions by Prost 1967 and Valenzuela and Iggesen 2007 record the same pitch prominence under the labels 'high pitch' and 'lexical accent', so the sources differ only in what they call it.

catalog_quote: The domain of stress assignment is the first two syllables of the root or prefix-root combination. If the root is only one syllable long, then the stress domain is extended to include a root+suffix combination or root+enclitic combination ... I will refer to this two syllable window as the stress domain. The rule of stress assignment is stated in (2.19). (2.19) Stress rule: a. Assign-to-H-tone: Assign stress to the syllable that contains a high tone in a two syllable window on the left edge of the stress domain. b. First-syllable-stress: If no high tone is present on the second syllable of the stress domain assign stress to the first syllable (or assign stress to the first syllable elsewhere). [p.85] ... When a syllable is stressed and toneless it is realized either with a low or a mid pitch as is represented in the example in (2.22). This example shows clearly that it is an overgeneralization to simply say that stress is attracted to all syllables with a high tone. It falls on the first syllable by default, and on the second syllable if there is a high tone present on this syllable. (2.22) [ˈhà.ná.yó.kɨ̀] / [hā.nà.yó.kɨ̀] hana=yó=kɨ leave=CMPL=DEC:P 'S/he left everything.' [p.88] ... Stress is obligatory (at least 1) and culminative (no more than 1) in the stress domain. There is one and only one stress in the two-syllable window of the stress domain. [p.91]
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Chácobo (chac1251) is not in the catalog. The single title-keyword item, Valenzuela & Iggesen 2007 'El desarrollo de un marcador suprasegmental en chácobo (pano)' (UCAB Caracas volume, pp.187-199, Spanish), has no open copy anywhere reachable (Crossref, OpenAlex, S2, archive.org, Dialnet, Chapman Digital Commons: nothing; Google/Scholar/Bing/DDG/HathiTrust/WorldCat/academia. The chapter is first-hand and does bear on word accent: it posits 'acento léxico' on the first or the second syllable of disyllabic nouns (plus trisyllabic nouns) and describes the ergative as 'un mecanismo puramente suprasegmental, la mudanza del acento a la última sílaba', derived diachronically from Proto-Pano *-n; its main object is the case exponent, not stress typology. Tallman's 2018 UT Austin grammar (held by the project from our earlier reading; §2.3 pp.84-101) is the authoritative statement: stress is predictable, on the first syllable of the stem by default and on the second when it carries a lexical H tone, obligatory and culminative in a two-syllable left-edge window, coexisting with privative H tone; instrumentally supported by Tallman & Elías-Ulloa 2020 (JASA, abstract only). Tallman reanalyses V&I's 'acento' as H tone and contradicts their aspect-split and apocope claims. Acquisition priority for V&I 2007: medium (a print-only 13-page chapter; the Spanish lexical-accent reading is already superseded by Tallman 2018 but is the only Valenzuela/Iggesen first-hand print statement); Tallman & Elías-Ulloa 2020 full text: medium.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Chácobo has a privative lexical high tone (H vs toneless) and a separate, predictable stress. Stress is computed over a two-syllable window at the left edge of the stem (root, or prefix+root; a monosyllabic root extends the window into the following suffix/enclitic): it falls on the second syllable if that syllable carries a high tone, otherwise on the first (stem-initial) syllable. Stress is obligatory and culminative within this domain; H tone is neither (several H tones may surface). A default H is inserted on the first syllable of an H-insertion domain when no H is present there, so stress and H often coincide. Acoustic correlates: stress = intensity (+pitch), H tone = F0 + vowel duration (Tallman & Elías-Ulloa 2020). Author labels the whole a 'mixed tone-stress system' and notes the phonetic separation of the two prominences is not fully settled.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; stress is culminative (exactly one) in the two-syllable stress domain and no rhythmic/secondary stress is mentioned anywhere in the grammar (the earlier foot-based analysis with M-toned secondary prominences, Tallman 2014/2017, is explicitly abandoned in fn.5 p.84).
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic roots extend the stress domain rightward into a suffix or enclitic; stressed toneless syllables surface with low or mid pitch (e.g. [ˈhà.ná.yó.kɨ̀] ~ [hā.nà.yó.kɨ̀]); Spanish loans treated separately (§2.4); earlier literature (Prost 1960/1967, Iggesen 2007) described three tones, which Tallman attributes to the pitch effects of stress on a one-tone system; Pacahuara co-dialect shows glottal-stop insertion after the first syllable of possibly prosodic origin (§1, p.35-36).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the stem (root or prefix+root), left edge — not the phonological word, which Tallman argues is not a motivated constituent in Chácobo; enclitics/suffixes fall outside the stress window except after monosyllabic roots. Statements are based on both elicited words and connected speech plus a 5-speaker production study; case-marking and phrase-level H tones (tone sandhi, ch.5-6) interact with but do not move stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Chácobo proper (chac1251, ISO cao) as spoken in Alto Ivón, Las Limas and other Beni communities; Tallman treats Pacahuara (paca1245, ISO pcp) as a co-dialect and notes minor prosodic differences (glottal-stop insertion after the first syllable), but the stress statement is for Chácobo. Note the analytical history: Tallman 2014/2017 (and González 2017 following him) described Chácobo as lexical-stress with stress-driven tone; the 2018 grammar and the 2020 JASA study replace this with privative lexical H tone plus predictable stem-initial (or H-attracted second-syllable) stress.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Within what the snippets expose, Prost gives no default word-stress placement rule. He lists Chácobo's phonemes in a footnote (segments only, referring to Prost 1960) and treats prominence grammatically: the transitive-subject (ergative) marker is a suprasegmental 'postposition' consisting of high pitch on the noun-final syllable (joni bo 'men' absolutive vs. joni bá 'men' transitive subject), with the plural allomorph bo/ba conditioned by unstressed vs. stressed position; trisyllabic class-I nouns instead lose their final syllable in absolutive (S of intransitive / O of transitive) position. 'High pitch' and 'stressed position' are used for the same phenomenon, i.e. Prost does not separate stress from pitch. Vol. I's notation legend uses three pitch levels (1 low, 2 mid, 3 high).
new_statements.exceptions: Class I nouns (trisyllables) mark absolutive position by eliding the final syllable rather than by the pitch contrast; class II = all other nouns. Nothing on default placement, so no exceptions to a placement rule are visible.
new_statements.identity_note: Prost describes the Chácobo of the Benicito, Ivon and Yata rivers (Beni, Vaca Diez province), i.e. the same variety Tallman 2018 documents; no separate dialect is named.

Prost's 'tono elevado' transitive-subject postposition is the 1965 attestation of the ergative floating H tone (Tallman 2018) / NP-final accent shift (Valenzuela & Iggesen 2007); on default stress placement the work is silent, so it neither confirms nor contradicts initial-default / second-if-H. Small locator correction to the record: the pospos inventory is p.121 (heading at the foot of p.120).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No phonology/stress section and no statement of where word stress falls (fn.1 gives the segment inventory only, referring implicitly to Prost 1960). What the Spanish original states, exactly as the 1967 English edition: a suprasegmental postposition ´ 'tono elevado' (high pitch) on the noun marks the transitive subject, and ´ (alone when not sentence-final, -´no sentence-finally) marks time/instrument/location; the plural enclitic is bo 'no acentuada' vs bá 'cuando va acentuada' (joni bo 'men' vs joni bá 'men, transitive subject'); a word-final unaccented vowel drops before another word; class I trisyllabic nouns elide their final syllable in S/O phrase-final position; the volume marks intonation with tone levels 1-3. Accented vs unaccented syllables and a grammatical high tone are thus presupposed, but default word-stress placement is never described.
new_statements.exceptions: none (no placement rule); morphophonemic noun class I (relative pronoun + trisyllabic nouns) loses its final syllable phrase-finally as intransitive S / transitive O and non-finally outside S/O phrases (§6.3.1 pp.127-128)
new_statements.identity_note: Prost describes Chácobo (Panoan) as spoken c. 1955-1965 by c. 155 speakers on the Benicito, Ivon and Yata rivers, Prov. Vaca Diez, Dept. Beni, Bolivia (p.285); same community as Tallman's (Alto Ivon region), two generations earlier. No Pacahuara material.

tone_statements.quote: Chácobo has a tonal system that distinguishes high tone marked syllables from toneless syllables. The tonal system is lexically contrastive (e.g. haná ‘vomit’ vs. hana ‘leave’; kaʂá ‘play’ vs. káʂa ‘be angry’). ... Chácobo is a tonal language with a distinction between high tones and toneless syllables. Toneless syllables are realized with a low pitch. ... Despite the simplicity of the tonal inventory tone insertion and tone sandhi rules are rather complex. ... Chácobo also displays stress marking.

tone_statements.summary: Privative lexical tone: high vs toneless (low-pitch) syllables, contrastive (haná 'vomit' vs hana 'leave'); H insertion and HH>LH sandhi; ergative marked by a bare high tone; separate stress.

readall_conflicts: No new contradiction. Prost 1965/1967 (snippets only) describe the ergative as 'high pitch' / 'tono elevado' on the noun-final syllable and speak of 'stressed vs. unstressed position' for the same phenomenon, which is the observation that Valenzuela & Iggesen 2007 later phrase as an accent shift to the NP-final syllable and that Tallman 2018 reanalyses as a floating H tone in a mixed tone-stress system with predictable stress in a two-syllable left-edge window. The only tension is terminological (Prost: pitch = stress; V&I: lexical accent; Tallman: tone plus predictable stress), not a disagreement about where the prominence sits. Nothing in the Prost snippets addresses the default initial stress, so Tallman 2018 remains the deciding source for placement. One caution: the Google Books passage 'Contour 1 = stress and mid or high tone on the penult.. of all phonemic words' belongs to a different language in Bolivian Indian Grammars II and must not be read as a Chácobo penultimate-stress statement.

sources.quote: The domain of stress assignment is the first two syllables of the root or prefix-root combination. [...] I will refer to this two syllable window as the stress domain. The rule of stress assignment is stated in (2.19). (2.19) Stress rule: a. Assign-to-H-tone: Assign stress to the syllable that contains a high tone in a two syllable window on the left edge of the stress domain. b. First-syllable-stress: If no high tone is present on the second syllable of the stress domain assign stress to the first syllable (or assign stress to the first syllable elsewhere). [p.85] ... It falls on the first syllable by default, and on the second syllable if there is a high tone present on this syllable. [p.88]

sources.note: Family-level statement only: contrastive high/low tone has been described for just three Panoan languages (Chakobo, Kapanawa of the Tapiche, Amawaka), plays a minor role even there, and is considered a recent Nawa-internal innovation rather than proto-Panoan; Katukina is not among the languages with described tone (no first-hand statement about Katukina prosody).
sources.venue: Anthropological Papers of the American Museum of Natural History

tone.quote: A few Panoan languages have been described as having contrastive high and low tones, specifically Chakobo (Prost, 1960: 8, 1962: 111, 1967: 64), Kapanawa of the Tapiche River (Loos, 1969: 186ff.), and Amawaka (Russell, 1958; Russell and Russell 1959). Unlike tonal languages in the vicinity, like Tikuna, Bora, and Witoto, in all Panoan languages where they have been described, these contrastive tones play only a minor role. Panoan tones appear to be recent innovations specific to these Nawa languages, rather than a proto-Panoan feature (see Loos, 1999b: 230).
